extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys/prosecutors)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural guidance for when an examiner may properly require restriction or election between claimed inventions (including Markush groups, transitional applications, nucleotide sequences, and reissue applications) during U.S. patent examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for imposing restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims of an application may properly be required to be restricted to one of two or more claimed inventions only if they are able to support separate patents and they are either independent or distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References MPEP §§ 802.01, 806.06, 808.01 for 'independent' and MPEP § 806.05–§ 806.05(j) for 'distinct'. The examiner must consider whether separate patents could be supported for the claimed inventions before requiring restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine all claims if no serious burden
rubrics_metrics.description: If the search and examination of all the claims in an application can be made without serious burden, the examiner must examine them on the merits, even though they include claims to independent or distinct inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restriction is inappropriate where combined search/examination does not impose a serious burden on the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part test for restriction between patentably distinct inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two criteria for a proper requirement for restriction between patentably distinct inventions: (A) the inventions must be independent or distinct as claimed; and (B) there would be a serious search and/or examination burden on the examiner if restriction is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both criteria must be satisfied to justify a restriction requirement; see MPEP § 803.02, § 808, and § 808.02 for establishing burden and distinctness details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence or distinctness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions must be independent (see MPEP § 802.01, § 806.06, § 808.01) or distinct as claimed (see MPEP § 806.05–§ 806.05(j)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the MPEP analyses for independence/distinctness (e.g., compare claimed subject matter, genus/species, combination/subcombination, related products/processes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious search or examination burden requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a serious search and/or examination burden on the examiner if restriction is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 803.02, 808, and 808.02 for how to demonstrate serious burden; burden can be prima facie shown and may be rebutted by applicant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must provide reasons/examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must provide reasons and/or examples to support conclusions for restriction, but need not cite documents to support the restriction requirement in most cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When plural inventions are related in more than one way, the examiner must demonstrate both applicable criteria for distinctness. Provide clear explanations on the record to justify restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not restrict when express admission of obviousness exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is an express admission that the claimed inventions would have been obvious over each other within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 103, restriction should not be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Lee, 199 USPQ 108 (Comm’r Pat. 1978) as authority; an admission of obviousness between claimed inventions negates the need for restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing of serious search burden (how to show)
rubrics_metrics.description: A serious search burden on the examiner may be prima facie shown by appropriate explanation of separate classification, or separate status in the art, or a different field of search as defined in MPEP § 808.02.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document which classifications/fields of search would be required for different inventions to justify that a serious search burden exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing of serious examination burden (how to show)
rubrics_metrics.description: A serious examination burden may be prima facie shown by appropriate explanation of non-prior-art issues under 35 U.S.C. 101, pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, and/or 35 U.S.C. 112(a) relevant to one invention that are not relevant to the other invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify substantive statutory issues unique to one claimed invention (e.g., 101 eligibility, written description, enablement) to demonstrate examination burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant may rebut prima facie burden showing
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie showing of serious search and/or examination burden may be rebutted by appropriate showings or evidence by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant submissions (arguments, evidence, amendments) can demonstrate that combined search/exam is not seriously burdensome; examiners should consider such rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claims: provisional election permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining a Markush claim, the examiner may generally require a provisional election of species from among patentably indistinct species or patentably indistinct groups of species. The applicant’s election serves as a starting point for the search and examination of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2117 for determination of proper Markush grouping and for improper grouping rejections; both an election requirement and an improper grouping rejection may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Markush grouping criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping is proper if: (1) the members of the Markush group share a 'single structural similarity,' and (2) the members share a common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Supplementary Examination Guidelines and In re Harnisch; when Markush describes part of a combination/process, members must be substitutable expecting the same intended result; for chemical compounds, consider the compound as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitutability in combination/process Markush groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Markush grouping describes part of a combination or process, the members following 'selected from the group consisting of' must be substitutable, one for the other, with the expectation that the same intended result would be achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Multilayer Stretch Cling Film Holdings v. Berry Plastics Corp.; ensure alternatives are actually alternatively usable for the invention's purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical Markush grouping: consider compounds as wholes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Markush grouping describes part of a chemical compound, the members need not share a community of properties themselves; the propriety is determined by a consideration of the compound as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Harnisch; do not break compounds into elements when evaluating propriety of grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush grouping rejection procedural timing
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on an improper Markush grouping should be made in an Office action on the merits. If a written provisional election of species requirement must be made separate from the first Office action on the merits, it should not include a rejection on the basis of an improper Markush grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both provisional election and improper grouping issues apply, handle the improper grouping as a merits rejection in the first Office action on the merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to require provisional election for Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim that includes a Markush grouping reads on two or more patentably distinct inventions, a provisional election of species requirement may be made at the examiner’s discretion, except if members are few or so closely related that search/exam can be made without serious burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require election between species that are not patentably distinct or when the Markush group is proper and causes no serious burden. Avoid inviting applicant to elect a group that would be clearly rejectable as improper or under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephonic election practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner chooses to require a provisional election of species, in most cases the examiner should call the applicant to request a telephonic election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant elects by telephone, use form paragraph 8.23 in the next Office action on the merits and note whether election was made with or without traverse; include form paragraph 8.23.01 if applicant declined telephone election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of provisional election and improper Markush grouping rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If a written provisional election of species requirement is made prior to the first Office action on the merits, it should not include an improper Markush grouping rejection. Any appropriate improper Markush grouping rejection should be made in an Office action on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep election and improper-markush rejection distinct in timing; if claim is amended to include improper grouping later, examiner may require provisional election in that same action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination begins after election; treatment of elected species rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination on the merits begins after the applicant’s election. If the elected species or group is anticipated or obvious over the prior art, an appropriate art-based rejection should be made and non-elected species held withdrawn from further consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also make non-prior-art rejections that apply to elected species. Treat elections made with traverse in accordance with MPEP § 821.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use form paragraph 8.40 for improper Markush grouping rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Markush grouping was improper, a rejection on that basis should be made using form paragraph 8.40 and advising which species do not belong to a proper Markush group including the elected species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper Markush grouping rejections are appealable, not petitionable; use the form paragraph to advise applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending search when elected species allowable within proper Markush grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: If the elected species is not anticipated/obvious, the examiner should extend the search and examination to a non-elected species or group that falls within the scope of a proper Markush grouping including the elected species until prior art is found or no prior-art rejection can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner need not extend search beyond a proper Markush grouping; continue examination for other patentability requirements (101, 112, double patenting, proper grouping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of record regarding species searched and provisional election status
rubrics_metrics.description: In the interest of compact prosecution, the examiner should ensure the record is clear as to which species have been searched and found allowable and should indicate if the provisional election requirement has been modified or withdrawn based on additional searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear recordkeeping is critical to proper application of 35 U.S.C. 121 in later divisional applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on requiring limitation of proper Markush group absent patentability rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may not seek to require an applicant to limit the scope of a claim directed to a proper Markush group to a subset of species that falls within the scope of the claim in the absence of a rejection of the claim for not complying with patentability requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use Ex parte Quayle actions or Notices of Non-Responsive Amendment to force such limitations without a patentability rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality of provisional election upon final rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Markush claim is rejected over prior art in a proper final rejection, the applicant’s provisional election loses its provisional status and is given full effect under 35 U.S.C. 121; the examiner need not continue to search the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include potential application of the 35 U.S.C. 121 shield in later divisional applications; applicants who elected with traverse may petition under 37 CFR 1.144 if requirement made final.

rubrics_metrics.name: No allowance of Markush claim until improper grouping resolved
rubrics_metrics.description: No Markush claim can be allowed until any improper Markush grouping rejection has been overcome or withdrawn and all other conditions of patentability have been satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure improper grouping issues are resolved on the record prior to allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional application restriction exceptions (37 CFR 1.129)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications pending at least three years as of June 8, 1995, no requirement for restriction or filing of divisional applications shall be made or maintained after June 8, 1995, except where: (i) requirement first made prior to April 8, 1995; (ii) examiner had not made a requirement prior to April 8, 1995 due to applicant actions; or (iii) required fee for examination of each additional invention was not paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.129(b) provides procedures to allow examination of more than one independent and distinct invention in certain older applications upon payment of fees; see details and exceptions in the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant options under 37 CFR 1.129(b)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application contains more than one independent and distinct invention and a restriction cannot be maintained under 1.129(b)(1), applicant will be notified and given time to: (i) elect the invention(s) to be searched/examined and pay fee for each additional invention; (ii) confirm an earlier election and pay fees; or (iii) file a petition traversing the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a timely petition defers the original time period for electing and paying fees; no petition fee is required under this paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of additional inventions if fees unpaid
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional inventions for which the required fee has not been paid will be withdrawn from consideration under 37 CFR 1.142(b). An applicant who desires examination of an invention so withdrawn can file a divisional application under 35 U.S.C. 121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform applicants that divisionals can be used to pursue withdrawn inventions; use form paragraph 8.41 to notify about transitional application status and fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of applicant actions preventing pre-1995 restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples constituting 'actions by the applicant' that could have prevented a restriction before April 8, 1995 include: abandoning and refiling such that no Office action could be issued; requesting suspension of prosecution; delaying presentation of claims to multiple inventions; combining several applications into one continuing application and delaying filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If present or parent application was on examiner’s docket for at least 3 months prior to abandonment/suspension or amendment was filed at least 3 months prior to April 8, 1995, those are prima facie evidence that applicant actions did not prevent restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional application refunds when linking/generic claim allowable
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever divided inventions in a transitional application are rejoined because a linking claim or a generic claim is allowable and applicant paid the fee for the additional invention/species, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP §§ 806.04(d), 821.04, and § 821.04(a) to determine when nonelected species are no longer withdrawn from consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nucleotide sequence restriction presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Polynucleotide molecules defined by their nucleic acid sequence that encode different proteins are structurally distinct chemical compounds and are thus deemed to normally constitute independent and distinct inventions within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent evidence to the contrary, each such nucleotide sequence is presumed to be independent/distinct and subject to restriction pursuant to 37 CFR 1.141 et seq.; historical waivers (1996) were later rescinded (2007). Supplemental restriction requirements will not ordinarily be advanced where action on the merits for multiple sequences has already occurred, absent extenuating circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue application restriction limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction in reissue applications may be required between subject matter of the original patent claims and previously unclaimed subject matter; restriction involving only subject matter of the original patent claims will not be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.176(b) governs: original patent claims must be examined together and, if restriction is required, the invention(s) of the original claims will be held constructively elected unless applicant files a disclaimer; non-elected inventions/distinct subject matter cannot be recovered by reissue if applicant previously acquiesced to a restriction and allowed patent on elected claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of acquiescing to restriction prior to reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Where restriction or election was made in an application and applicant permitted the elected invention to issue as a patent without filing a divisional on the non-elected invention(s), the non-elected inventions and non-claimed distinct subject matter cannot be recovered by filing a reissue application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing more than one reissue application (dividing reissue claims) is available under 37 CFR 1.177, but failure to timely file a divisional is not considered error correctable by reissue.
